[[RunningHead]]

Tessa Adams 1938-2017

Martin Stanton

Martin Stanton

martinstanton84@gmail.com

Martin Stanton  

I first met Tessa Adams at the University of Kent in Canterbury in March 1991. Tessa had just presented a summary of her doctoral thesis, ‘Creative experience and the “authenticity” of psychoanalytic discourse’, to a graduate research seminar at the Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies (CPS). In her paper, Tessa focused on the process of abjection - Julia Kristeva's term for somatic horror produced by the collapse of meaning - to gain a contextual sense of the interface between terror and ecstasy that philosophers like Hume and Kant link to the sublime. A few months later, Tessa was able to discuss her new ideas directly with Kristeva at a CPS workshop on depression (Adams, 2010). In under a year, Tessa emerged from her doctoral research with a major life topic - the sublime - and the creative setting in which she might best picture it - the snowcapped mountain range in the midst of existential Winter (aka depression).

Tessa realized soon after that this project could never be long confined within her doctoral thesis. This was rather the start of a live adventure with a haunting melody: the mountain sublime. This was Tessa's Spring. This was her steep upwards climb. Tessa clearly held all the peaks firmly in sight and mind. Nothing was going to prevent her from reaching them. Nothing did stop her until she was tragically struck down by Pick's disease in her final years.

Post-Kent, Tessa launched a clinical training in psychoanalytic counselling at Goldsmiths, University of London. A member of the Guild of Psychotherapists, she developed this alongside the art and group therapy training at Goldsmiths. This challenging and creative interface soon became a focal point for academic life - not least through the lively ongoing debate between Tessa and Dianne Waller on what constituted common ground between creative art and therapy. Tessa's passionate commitment to open non-sectarian debate - rare in clinical trainings even today - was particularly evident in her ongoing cooperation with Leon Schlamm for the Kent-based CPS Jung Studies Days in the 1990s. She helped Leon and others initiate debate on the creative impact of Jung on psychoanalysis, not least in the elaboration of foundational notions like the ‘complex’, ‘free association’ and the ‘imago’. This collaborative work helped inspire Tessa's seminal collection, The Feminine Case: Jung, Aesthetics and Creative Process, which she co-edited with Andrea Duncan (Adams and Duncan, 2003).

The Intricate Process of Psychoanalytic Research: Encountering the Intersubjective Experience of the Researcher-Participant Relationship

Clare Harvey

Clare Harvey

Private Bag 3, WITS, 2050, South Africa clare.harvey@wits.ac.za

Clare Harvey   Clinical psychologist, lecturer and researcher in the Psychology Department at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa. Her research interests are primarily in disability studies and motherhood, and she is currently completing her PhD entitled ‘Mothering a child with a physical disability: A psychoanalytic exploration of maternal subjectivity and meaning making’. She has published both locally and internationally, including in the journal Disability & Society. She has presented at numerous national and international conferences, including at the 9th Biennial International Society of Critical Health Psychology Conference (July 2015). She also reviews for various journals, including the accredited African Journal of Disability.
INTERSUBJECTIVITY, RESEARCHER-PARTICIPANT, RELATIONSHIP, DISABILITY, PSYCHOANALYTICALLY INFORMED, RESEARCH INTERVIEW, INTERSUBJECTIVE IDENTIFICATIONS, PSYCHOANALYTIC-RESEARCHER THIRDNESS

Qualitative research in general and the psychoanalytically informed research interview method specifically, can be emotionally demanding on researchers as they form relationships with participants. This is especially the case when researchers and participants share particular identities and experiences. In this paper I reflect on my experience of interviewing mothers raising children with a visible physical disability about their maternal subjectivity. At times this was an emotionally demanding and ethically challenging process as participants closely identified with certain aspects of my identity, particularly with my visible physical disability and motherhood peculiarities. Often participants unexpectedly reversed our roles, asking me intimate questions. I will deliberate these dilemmas using interview material. I argue for a mindful blurring with participants when this occurs. Using certain psychoanalytic-researcher concepts of inter subjectivity, transference-countertransference and psychoanalytic-researcher thirdness helped me successfully navigate these encounters. I will also explore the rich participant psychic functioning that was generated from this intersubjective relationship between myself and the participants.

Reflection

Judith Warren

Judith Warren

Judith Warren  

‘To whom shall I give my nice new little book polished dry with pumice?’ wrote Catullus - a question authors and editors continue to ask, the world over!

A review of a book of is deep importance to an author, as an acknowledgement of the work, as an expression of hoped-for understanding and, at best, illumination. I am only too aware that BJP can review but a handful of the published titles in the field. So here, in valediction, I would like to salute the books which it has not been possible to review during my watch, as well as those which have, and to honour the effort to clarify and communicate which a book represents. Reviewers for BJP, I have come to recognize, fully understand an author's large endeavour, and give generously of their time to read, write and, not least, submit to the yoke of both word count and editorial amendment.

In a scholarly and clinical journal, a review carries the responsibility of offering, where possible, both a critical, qualitative appraisal and an engaging entree to the title. I've tried to bring about that combination. Now our incoming editor, Poul Rohleder, will bring his own shaping spirit to the task, and I know he will be well assisted in the role. I have met with great patience and kindness from colleagues, and have been particularly supported by Ann Scott, previous reviews editor Liane Aukin, and fellow members of the Editorial Board. My grateful thanks, of course, to all who have written reviews, and to everyone who has given me advice and suggestions along the way. I've enjoyed the post, and hope that something of that pleasure has been reflected in the pages I've worked on for BJP.

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

[a.sabbadini@gmail.com]

Andrea Sabbadini  

Originally coming out in Italy in 2014, we welcome the publication in English of this new book by the prominent Italian psychoanalyst Dr Cosimo Schinaia. I have found its title to be somewhat reductive, as the text actually covers a much wider range of topics than Psychoanalysis and Architecture, all of them nevertheless relevant to the practitioners of both these disciplines.

In fact I think this book will be of interest to all those for whom psychoanalysis is more than just a therapeutic profession, as indeed it was for Freud himself, but also a method of inquiry into the ever-surprising functionings of the mind - a tool for the interpretation of a vast variety of human activities, including and especially the creative ones - among which, of course, architecture (‘a frontier profession’ according to Renzo Piano) is here given a place of priority.

Schinaia emphasizes throughout these pages his ‘continuous need to connect the inside and the outside, psychical reality with physical reality’ (p. xxiii). Theoretical frameworks borrowed from the history of art, linguistics, aesthetics, philosophy, literature and, of course, psychoanalysis and architecture pervade the book, with a plethora of quotations from an impressive, and occasionally disconcerting, range of authors.

Chapter 1 (‘The origins of a meeting’) considers the practical and emotional implications of migration, including the author's own from Taranto in southern Italy to Genoa (he calls it, with reference to Kavafis' famous poem, ‘my Ithaca’), the city where he has been living and working for many years as a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst.

Elsewhere Schinaia focuses on what he describes as the ‘fertile connections and fruitful contaminations’ (p. 17)

Time-limited Psychodynamic Psychotherapy with Children and Adolescents: An Interactive Approach by Ruth Schmidt Neven. Published by Routledge, London, 2016; 154 pp, £24.99 paperback

Peter Wilson

Peter Wilson

[peterjbwilson@btinternet.com]

Peter Wilson  

Long-term psychoanalytical psychotherapy, thorough and necessary though it may well be for many, does not suit our times, hurried, impatient and hyper-managed as they are in the realm of social and health provision. It does not sit well in the public health arena in which the mental health needs of populations are now well known to far exceed the supply of appropriate services. Child and adolescent mental health services, forever chronically underfunded, are having a particularly hard time, carrying unbearable strain in the prevailing climate of serious cutbacks in health and social services. It cannot be of any surprise that local commissioners of services, transfixed as they are with trimming budgets, should now welcome recent so-called ‘transformations’ in these services, predominantly based as they are on brief cognitive behaviour therapies, supposedly cheaper and more effective. The commissioners' plain message to psychodynamic therapists is to speed up or else (your job is on the line). And so those who are having to listen are busy doing whatever they can to sharpen up their short-term psychotherapy skills.

The arrival of this book is thus timely. The author, who has extensive experience in the field of child and adolescent mental health, has taken up the challenge and has done so with force. Of course, she is aware of all the ravages of costcutting, but she is emphatic that what she has in mind with her version of time-limited psychodynamic psychotherapy is not a watered down solution, distorted for the purpose of survival. It is rather a distinct form of therapy that stands in its own right in clear contrast to other more fashionable approaches. She is dismissive of the biomedical approach with its emphasis on psychiatric diagnosis of individual children at the expense of due consideration being given to the relational, family and social context in which children live. She is set against providing any kind of manualized prescriptive procedures which she sees as antithetical to the whole spirit of psychodynamic psychotherapy.

Clare Harris  

I very much appreciate the generosity of the clinician in offering this interesting material for comment. Inevitably, a brief history and single session must leave out much from a therapy which has been ongoing for several years. In approaching it, I am interested in what might be the most immediate transference/countertransference dynamic at this point and in how that might be apprehended not only in the session but in the presentation as a whole.

On reading and rereading the material, I found myself with many questions: why this patient and why now? Has some nodal point been reached, that the therapist chooses to present him to us now? How many years is several - is it four or ten, or more? Where does the patient come in his family? What are his relationships like with his mother, his father, his siblings, beyond his enormous struggle to establish a life of his own? What does ‘a complex Holocaust history’ mean?

Psychoanalysis in the Age of Totalitarianism edited by Matt ffytche and Daniel Pick. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 2016; 287 pp; £120 (hardback); £31.99 (paperback)

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Canterbury, UK jvs@kent.ac.uk

Janet Sayers  

What was the two-way traffic between psychoanalysis and totalitarianism in the years between the installation of Hitler as Chancellor of Germany in 1933 and the execution of the Nazi Holocaust organizer, Adolf Eichmann, in 1962? This is the question Matt ffytche and Daniel Pick seek to answer with the chapters they bring together in this book.

It begins with the historian, Joel Isaac, explaining that ‘the origins of the idea of totalitarianism’ are linked with ‘the total penetration of the human subject by the state or party’ (p. 22). The term ‘totalitarian’, he says, was first coined in Italy in 1923. It was subsequently used, as the sociologist Michael Rustin points out in another chapter, by Friedrich Hayek in 1944, by Karl Popper in 1945, and by subsequent commentators as means of analysing and justifying, in the name of freedom and democracy, resistance to the Nazi regime of Hitler and to the Soviet regime of Stalin. The term was also used, says Rustin, to warn against milder forms of political collectivism or socialism.

So how have the ideas of totalitarianism and psychoanalysis interacted? In answering this question Stephen Frosh highlights the way that, in the late 1940s, the psychoanalytic theory of repression and projection was used to explain psychological adherence to Nazi totalitarianism and anti-Semitism. Ffytche in turn draws attention to ways in which susceptibility to fascist and totalitarian propaganda was explained psychoanalytically by Frankfurt School sociologists in terms of early childhood submission to the father and to other father-like figures beyond the family.

Many readers might be familiar with this interaction between totalitarianism and psychoanalysis. New to me is material in subsequent chapters about ways in which psychoanalysis was used before, during, and following the second world war to combat totalitarianism. Ffytche and Pick include in this category a chapter by Michael Shapira about the work of psychoanalysts, involved with the London-based Institute for the Scientific Treatment of Delinquency, geared to developing criminological approaches to antisocial behaviour along psychotherapeutic lines. I was also intrigued by ways, documented in a chapter by Dagmar Herzog, in which totalitarianism, or at least the seeming justification of its violence provided by Konrad Lorenz's theory of innate aggression, was countered psychoanalytically in post-war Germany. Also noteworthy is Sally Alexander's chapter highlighting the democratic vision of the British psychoanalyst, Donald Winnicott; his warning against condemning democracy's enemies without acknowledging totalitarian traits within oneself; and his observations regarding fear of ‘absolute dependence’ on the mother as cause of ‘the dictator's will to power’ (p. 118).

Commentary by a Member of the Bowlby Centre

Mark Linington

Mark Linington

[mark.linington@btinternet.com]

Mark Linington  

It is an especially satisfying experience to hear about another psychotherapist's clinical work, especially when, as here with Maria, the psychotherapist has presented his/her work in such an open and detailed way, providing us with moving and interesting material. However, it is also worth acknowledging that face-to-face attunement is not possible when providing a commentary on another psychotherapist's written clinical material. When one is engaged in a dialogue with colleagues about their clinical work, we are all the time making judgements about their readiness to explore the significance of what they are describing. At the same time, we are also judging whether they wish to take a step back from such consideration of their work, and perhaps whether our treatment of their work and themselves seems to need protection from what may feel like an intrusion. In addition, the commentator and psychotherapist do not know each other: they have not built up a relationship secure enough from which to explore. Feelings regarding such issues, which arise face-to-face, are significant not only for gauging the helpfulness or otherwise of particular aspects of exploration, but are also useful as a source of parallel process information (Searles, 1955). I have noticed these issues especially coming to my mind when considering my response to this clinical material, which contains signs of significant distress. It may not be coincidental that these relational themes are themselves present in the clinical material presented here: the difficulties for the psychotherapist in attuning, the question of how to establish sufficient security to allow for exploratory thinking, and the difficulties for the patient in having a two-person relationship (Aron, 1990).

I am an attachment-based psychoanalytic psychotherapist and supervisor with The Bowlby Centre in London. Attachment-based psychoanalytic psychotherapy focuses on the need of patients to develop a secure base with the psychotherapist (Bowlby, 1988) in order to begin to explore reflectively their current and past ways of relating. In these explorations attention is given to both real experiences of attachment trauma and the links to ways in which these experiences currently operate unconsciously, both internally and externally. Attachment trauma can include experiences of acute and chronic dismissiveness and neglect, anxious self-preoccupation on the part of the caregiver, or sustained aggression or fearfulness. Relational security is developed with another through a process of attunement, mis-attunement and repair, the regulation of the fear system, and the development of effective careseeking (McCluskey, 2005). A key issue in the clinical work with patients who have experienced significant attachment trauma, which has left them with an ongoing particular form of fearfulness in relationships (as with Maria), is how to establish enough safety with the caregiver. If such safety can be established, there is the possibility that the new care and closeness offered can be taken in as a source of relief from distress, and a new opportunity for vitality can be enjoyed (Heard, Lake & McCluskey, 2009).

The Shadow of the Second Mother: Nurses and Nannies in Theories of Infant Development by Prophecy Coles. Published by Routledge, London, 2015; 136 pp, £26.99 paperback

Joanna Ryan

Joanna Ryan

London
joannaryan@blueyonder.co.uk

Joanna Ryan  

In this wide ranging book, Prophecy Coles approaches the highly contested subject of delegated mothering. Highly contested because it is often impossible not to take one of two opposing and dogmatic views, that of the putatively injured child whose mother is absent from her daily life, or that of the needs and aspirations of the mother. Highly contested also because it is mainly the children of the relatively privileged who receive such substitute care from nannies, women of lesser social and economic status (which of course ignores all those children from poorer families who may be fostered or adopted, or cared for by child-minders). However, many of our patients in private practice will have received extensive delegated mothering, and Coles' book depicts the many ramifications of this in their internal worlds. She also shows the limitations of psychoanalytic theory and practice in any adequate recognition of the non-biological care taker or substitute parent, something which has a wider relevance.

Freud famously said of his nurse: ‘… The prime originator [of my troubles] was a woman, ugly, elderly but clever…’. He followed this a few paragraphs later with: ‘(I)f I succeed in resolving my own hysteria, I shall be grateful to the old woman who provided me at such an early age with the means for living and going on living. As you see my old liking for her is breaking through again’ (Freud, 1897, pp. 261-2). However, in the same sequence of letters to Fliess, and after recounting the degree of his emotional disturbance at his nurse's sudden dismissal, Freud rapidly disavowed the psychic importance of such figures, in his formulation of the Oedipus complex and its restriction to the biological parents only. In such ways (and there are many other instances, as I argue in Ryan (2017)) was the significance of the working-class nurse eclipsed by the often idealized and more distant mother. There is now a considerable secondary literature on how Freud's nurse continued to haunt his dreams, the vague ‘impression’ that Coles suggests he was left with. Freud also wrote to Fliess that such employees were ‘worthless female material’, and later to Jung that they were inadequate as psychoanalytic subjects themselves: ‘… one can learn nothing from them’ (Freud, 1907, p. 64).

Robert Snell

Robert Snell

London
[r.snell@tiscali.co.uk]

Robert Snell  

A key premise of this bracing book is that ‘inner’ and ‘outer’ interact and shape each other. Severing the two - as Rod Tweedy writes in his intelligent introduction - has led ‘to a devitalised and dissociated form of politics, and to a disengaged and disempowering form of therapy and analysis’ (p. xxvi). The book offers multiple (but not, surprisingly, group analytic) perspectives on how we are, already and necessarily, ‘political selves’. Therapy and analysis are in central focus, starting with Andrew Samuels' foreword, which lists ways in which the terms ‘psychotherapy’ and ‘politics’ tend to be linked; the ‘mental illness’ of the title, invoked so uncritically, might suggest a book of narrower scope.

The stage is set in the late David Smail's opening essay: we are each ‘a point in social space-time through which powers flow’ (p. 19). Psychotherapy, ‘one of the greatest cultural and commercial success stories of the Western world’ (p. 3), has, from Freud onwards, sought the reasons for distress within rather than outside the person. It is pulled to this position, and sealed off from the rest of reality, through the action of its own ‘interest’ (p. 6). A change of perspective is needed, in which motivation is seen not as driven internally but pulled from outside, socially and environmentally. Otherwise, we are stuck with ‘magical voluntarism’ (p. 10), the idea that it is up to us individually - with the help of a therapist, of course - to change things. Smail excoriates therapeutic ‘scientism’, CBT, ‘the myth of mental illness’, the ‘psychotic’ idea that we are merely the stories we tell about ourselves, and humanist therapies in general. Neither can much be expected from psychoanalysis, thanks to its founder's irredeemable conservatism; attempts like the Frankfurt School's to marry Freud and Marx are doomed.

Joel Kovel would disagree. His closely argued ‘Therapy in late capitalism’, first published in 1976-7, is a touchstone for the rest of the book. Kovel and Smail would concur on some things: therapy is a political, materially based act. Neurosis is ‘a structure grounded on a nodal point in subjectivity and extending beyond the individual to encompass the entirety of his social relations’. But at its heart is ‘the intrusion of incompletely repressed fantasy’ (p. 44): psychoanalysis underpins Kovel's thinking from the start. Neurosis in capitalism is ubiquitous, for capitalism catches us all between the demands of reason and of desire: on the one hand, ‘the fetishism of commodities’, the reality principle of capital that requires a standard of objective rationality so that we can exchange things; and on the other hand, the deeper layers of desiring, recalcitrant subjectivity. Work, increasingly, is the cultivation of human relations themselves, which become technical.

Rosemary Rizq

Rosemary Rizq   Chartered psychologist, an HCPC-registered counselling psychologist and a UKCP-registered psychoanalytic psychotherapist. She is Principal Lecturer in Counselling Psychology at the University of Roehampton and until recently worked as specialist lead for research and development for NHS Ealing. She now works as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist for North-East London NHS Foundation Trust and has a part-time private practice in West London. She was submissions editor for Psychodynamic Practice from 2004 to 2010, is a reviewer for a number of academic journals and she has published widely on issues related to organizational dynamics and psychotherapeutic training and practice. Recent key papers include: ‘IAPT anxiety and envy’, ‘The perversion of care’, ‘States of abjection’ and ‘The ghost in the machine’.

Isak Dinesen's novella Babette's Feast tells the story of how a small, quarrelsome Lutheran community in Norway comes to be transformed by the arrival of a stranger, the French cook Babette. In her deceptively simple tale, Dinesen adopts explicitly Eucharistic language and imagery to convey the connection between eating and faith, exploring via rich use of metaphor the way in which we come to be inhabited and nourished by the other. In this paper, I follow Dinesen's sacramental perspective by offering the Catholic notion of transubstantiation as a model for furthering psychoanalytic theorizing about the presence of the other within. Following an outline of Dinesen's story, I draw on work by Freud, Abraham and Torok, and Kristeva to explore differing notions of unconscious identification, incorporation and the metaphorical basis of subjectivity. I develop these ideas through a discussion of the central celebratory dinner given by Babette and conclude by considering some of the implications of the story for psychoanalytic practice.

Karl Abraham: Life And Work, A Biography by Anna Bentinck van Schoonheten. Published by Karnac, London, 2016; xxiii + 432 pp, £35 hardback

Ken Robinson

Ken Robinson

ken25rob@gmail.com

Ken Robinson  

Although Karl Abraham is a pivotal figure in psychoanalysis, his work is more referred to than read. Perhaps this is because he died prematurely, perhaps it is because he has tended, certainly in British psychoanalytic thinking, to be acknowledged as the second analyst of Melanie Klein at the expense of the distinctiveness of his own work. Whatever the case, he has found more recent commentators in, for example, Good (1995), May (2001, 2012) and Sanfeliu (2014); and now in Anna Bentinck van Schoonheten's biography. None is British, which might tell its own story. Abraham awaits a British interpreter who will situate him within the wider history of British psychoanalysis and tease out his enduring influence, transmitted initially through those whom he analysed and helped to form, not only Melanie Klein but in particular Edward Glover who was on his couch, and Ella Sharpe and Sylvia Payne who became intimate with his work when they were in analysis with Abraham's colleague, Hanns Sachs, in Berlin. All exercised a marked influence on the development of psychoanalysis in Britain as analysts and trainers. (Alix Strachey, another analysand, had a different influence as a translator.)

Abraham's death on Christmas day 1925 profoundly shocked his colleagues in the psychoanalytic movement. Freud took ill and remained unwell with various symptoms through to the Spring. In one of his Rundbriefe to the Secret Committee (20 January 1926) Freud described the loss as so crippling that he now found it difficult to turn his attention to other things: they seemed of no importance. As Freud and others, especially Ernest Jones, lamented, they had lost a man of extraordinary qualities, personally, politically and professionally. Upright, honest and loyal, Abraham was also a cool-headed diplomat within often heated psychoanalytic politics, and he had played a major, if understated, role in advancing psychoanalytic understanding. His work was still in process. By the time of his death Berlin had become the most creative and vibrant centre for psychoanalysis.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

Since its inception, the BJP's Rozsika Parker Prize has given authors scope to address questions of creativity in clinical work or in the application of psychoanalytic thinking to culture and the arts. Both winners in the 2016 Prize, published in this issue, consider clinical questions through an aesthetic lens, doing so in an imaginative way that greatly impressed our Judges. Benjamin Robinson (Student Path) approaches the writing-up of sessions as a ‘challenge of representation’ that can be addressed with methods appropriated from aesthetic theory, allowing for a ‘free-flowing write-up of the session, both creatively rich and clinically accurate’. Sian Ellis (Post-Qualification Path) considers the multidirectional movement of transference and countertransference in the supervisory situation, this time with the supervisor as a ‘point of origin, rather than the recipient’ of these dynamics, and in particular in relation to a dimension of translucent space that values the space for ‘imagining and dreaming’.

Our Research strand offers a subtle account of a qualitative research enquiry in which both the researcher and the children of the research subjects have a visible physical disability. Clare Harvey argues that a ‘mindful use of intersubjective identifications between researcher and participant’ is needed in order to conduct ethical qualitative research; and further that this is made possible through consciously working with transference-countertransference processes.

Two papers follow, in our regular Clinical and Theoretical Practice strand. Alina Schellekes, in a rich meditation on time, suggests that ‘deciphering the way the patient experiences time (and space) gives us an additional key to primitive areas of the psyche which do not express themselves in the usual verbal or symbolic ways’. Hanoch Yerushalmi takes up the question of ‘spontaneous developmental changes’ within analytic therapy, compassionately placing these within the conceptual framework of the ‘two types of basic forces’ working within the therapeutic setting: ‘regressive and progressive inner pressures’.

Michael Halton

Michael Halton

London mi.halton@btinternet.com

Michael Halton  

This is an ambitious and always thought-provoking book that goes far beyond what the subtitle How to Develop as a Psychoanalytic Practitioner suggests, and it has more than a hint of a moral agenda. In many ways it speaks to two audiences which Spurling addresses as two distinct groups with different degrees of clinical experience. However, it might equally address one group who are in two alternating states of mind; namely one state of mind where confidence and complacent certainty reigns and the other where doubt and helplessness has dominion. Hopefully whether one belongs to the experienced group of clinicians Spurling is principally addressing or the less experienced group, from time to time we all have the conviction that we are mere beginners and this is accompanied by moments of serious self-doubt. This is to be welcomed, as self-doubt when it is not under the dominance of an ego-destructive super ego can inoculate us periodically from the ever present dangers of omnipotence and omniscience.

Spurling is alert to the twin dangers of both debilitating destructive self-doubt and the routine autopilot use of psychoanalytic cliches. He devotes a good deal of useful space to clearly explicating the process and journey involved in the effort to gain experience by the qualified yet relative beginner in psychotherapy. He sympathetically describes the struggles of those who have established a bit of a foothold in analytic theory and practice, and have made some slow, painful progress towards acquiring a modicum of psychotherapeutic skill. Yet at the same time he simultaneously takes on and challenges many of the familiar concepts, shibboleths and bits of received wisdoms that are the currency of all of us, including the more senior.

This approach will bring deserved comfort to the self-doubters, whether they be in the experienced senior group or not, and hopefully it will stimulate critical self-examination and self-reflection among the more sophisticated and more confident, whether their confidence is deserved or part self-deception. Spurling gives the impression in his writing that he has managed to retain his humility while also combining it with a degree of confidence that can only come with time and repeated exposure to clinical experience, and this is evident as his discussion moves flexibly between these two poles.

Treating People with Psychosis in Institutions. A Psychoanalytic Perspective by Belinda S. Mackie. Published by Karnac, London, 2016; 296 pp, £24.74 paperback

John Gale

John Gale

johngaleuk@gmail.com

John Gale  

We are probably more aware now than in the past that organizations are often places that effortlessly manage to bring out the worst in people. The sadistic impulses that previously we thought only existed elsewhere have now been shown to be entwined in the heart of those institutions that purport to protect and care for our psychic as well as our bodily distress. Indeed, it could be argued that in mental health services, violence has often been systematized.

In the interwoven ‘places’ of psychosis and psychoanalysis we inevitably find the institution saturated in mythologies that have been fabricated to produce severely distorted histories. This, if we are to believe Roland Barthes, is in part because all texts are woven (texere). What Freudian discourse adds to this insight, reversing the Homeric principle, is that weaving always belongs to the night. The dream, that is to say, is an analogue of writing. Conflicts and deception are spun into literature and this includes the literature that institutions manufacture indirectly as well as directly. Psychoanalysis itself has produced diverse institutions of its own - schools, theoretical allegiances, authorizing bodies, and local and national organizations. Thus a psychoanalytic perspective on institutions is in itself a complex notion. But the title of this study is deceptive. The book does more than look psychoanalytically at institutions that treat those with a psychosis, although it does this in Chapter 4. It also reviews, in Chapters 6-9, some of the institutions which follow or followed a psychoanalytic methodology, however elastically that is understood. The institutions that the author has selected for consideration are listed at the back of the book (pp. 229-30). This makes it immediately clear where the author's sympathies lie.

After an introduction that outlines the conceptual framework of the book, the tale that Belinda Mackie tells in the preliminary chapter on psychiatry and psychoanalysis is one in which successive developments in psychiatry and schisms within psychoanalysis form the subtext. In this regard, one thing should not go unnoticed.

Ann Scott  

The new series of twice-yearly Clinical Commentaries is now established as a significant feature of the Journal. In this issue the narrative concerns once-weekly work with a 30-year-old female patient suffering from compulsive and obsessional neurosis. There is - naturally - close attention to the words spoken, the patient's inner stances, and, on this occasion, a difficult countertransference. The author of the clinical material writes that an intense transference developed, ‘as if we were a mother and child who were very close but in a claustrophobic way’. Our three respondents speak from interestingly different perspectives. The first, an attachment-based psychoanalytic psychotherapist, attends to this intensity as ‘indicative of the severity of an attachment trauma’; the second, from a Middle Group/Relational perspective, considers the possibility, among other things, that the therapist might be erring on the side of keeping the patient as a ‘fearful, dependent, fused child’; the third, within a Kleinian/object relations framework, focuses on the movement of object relations in the here-and-now of the session, noting the shift from ‘interruption’ to ‘development’ of the work.

In the last issue I mentioned the way in which winning authors in the 2016 Rozsika Parker Prize approached clinical questions through an aesthetic lens. This dual perspective is also found in Ian S. Miller's consideration of one- and two-person psychologies in reading and psychoanalysis, with particular reference to Samuel Beckett's work. This fine paper was Commended in the 2016 competition.

Our next paper, Nathan M. Szajnberg's detailed analysis of Winnicott's Piggle, published to mark the 40th anniversary of the publication of the book on the case, follows the BJP‘s posthumous publication of Christopher Reeves’ two-part discussion of the case two years ago. In suggesting that there are Kleinian and Anna Freudian elements of technique in Winnicott's way of working, Szajnberg offers a complex and thought-provoking paper.

We are delighted to present the third Clinical Commentary of this new series and are grateful to the psychotherapist who has offered clinical material and to the three commentators.

Clinical Material

Both my patient and I were born in Europe and we share a mother tongue in which the therapy is conducted. Early on, I suggested that she might benefit from coming more frequently but she responded as if she had not heard my suggestion, and I thought that the idea seemed so odd to her that there was no chance for her to take it in and consider it. She has now been coming once weekly for a year.

Maria (not her real name) has been taking medication for compulsive and obsessional neurosis since she was 20. She is now 30. Her compulsive thoughts centre on being a disappointment to others, especially her mother, or a bad employee, a bad daughter. She arrived in the UK three years ago.

During her first session, I got the picture of a patient who was totally psychically merged with her mother. It was difficult to tell which were her words and which her mother's. Maria said that she didn't allow herself to express the smallest criticism of her mother, and asked: ‘Am I right to talk about my mother here at all?’ A moment later she expressed a shy wish to separate from her enough to have a life of her own.

Maria's mother is a retired professional who suffers with anxiety neurosis, as did her maternal grandmother. This grandmother's sister committed suicide. Maria tried to present her childhood as bright and colourful, but gradually I heard that she had often seen her mother very unwell during her breakdowns. She describes her father as ‘a nut’, an asocial and autistic person. Her older brother has serious emotional difficulties and an alcohol addiction. He still lives with their parents. Maria is bisexual, and lives with her female partner.

A. Napier

A. Napier

[d.napier@ucl.ac.uk]

A. Napier  

Warren Colman has written a highly thoughtful and stimulating book not only about C.G. Jung's views and those of his followers on the meaning and function of archetypes, but more generally on the longstanding anthropological question of how shared meaning emerges, sustains itself, and is transformed over time. The book, therefore, is not only a deep dive into what may drive primordial imagery to transcend local values and cultural practices, but also an anthropological inquiry into what sustains those images locally in the psychological lives of individuals who invariably shape symbols to make meaning.

The level of erudition required to address such key issues in the history of social theory and analytical psychology is potentially overwhelming. But in this volume Colman does a remarkable job of reviewing the relevant arguments on collective meaning that emerge from quite diverse fields of research and practice. These include not only the central places of analytical psychology and social anthropology in this study, but also history, linguistics, philosophy, ethology, paleontology, and neuroscience, to name a few.

What is at stake in this book is enormous. But to sense its scope is not only to understand key problems in the history of analytical psychology. It also means understanding key problems in the history of social theory, and especially the impact of French social theory on Jung's early, and still nascent, views. For a battle was also raging in the social sciences during the early twentieth century over Lucien Lévy-Bruhl's concept of participation mystique and the degree to which one could ever understand the diverse forms of awareness and systems of value evidenced in other societies, and especially those forms of embodied engagement that were not merely conscious or psychologically malleable in the analytical sense.

In fact, Lévy-Bruhl's ideas about social participation had, as Robert Segal has shown, a significant impact on Jung's views of shared meaning and how it emerges in collective representations. Indeed, it is this last issue of embodied imagination that Colman rightly identifies as needing considerable unpacking, and to which much of this book is devoted. However, to do this, Colman must first examine the basis of Jung's famously controversial view that, because archetypes pattern behaviour over generations, a scientific psychology should acknowledge them as also at some level biological.

DISABILITY PSYCHOTHERAPY, COMPULSIVE SPITTING, CLASSICAL FRAME, TALKING CURE

Every practicing psychotherapist will have ample experience of patients expressing rage and hatred during the course of a session. In virtually all cases, patients emit their fury in a verbal form. But what happens when an angry, traumatized patient lacks the capacity to spit out nasty words and, instead, spits saliva? While most adult psychotherapy patients have developed a well-internalized ability to keep their bodily fluids contained inside their bodies (with the possible exception of tears), severely and profoundly learned disabled patients can drool, vomit, urinate, defecate, ejaculate, and spit in the midst of a psychotherapy session. In view of this little-discussed, yet not infrequent, clinical phenomenon, how can a psychotherapist function when under attack from the patient and his or her actual bodily fluids? In order to explore this aspect of disability psychotherapy, the author will discuss an eight-year treatment with a psychotic, brain-damaged psychogeriatric patient who spat compulsively in an aggressive manner. The author will describe the way in which he endeavoured to use classical psychoanalytical approaches in order to create an environment of safety in which the patient could begin to experience greater mental containment as well as bodily containment, and eventually arrive at a state in which her spittle could be transformed into feelings and even rudimentary words.

The ‘I’ of Elephants and Eyes: Psychotic Signification and Psychoanalysis

Jenny Watson

Jenny Watson

Jenny Watson   Pseudonym. The author has a background in philosophy and poetry and has taught extensively in schools and universities. She is a published poet and freelance writer. Address for correspondence: c/o Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, BJP. [bjp@ann-scott.net]
LACAN, PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOSIS, PHILOSOPHY, TRAUMA, METAPHOR, METONYMY

Writing as an analysand I argue that without psychoanalytic support psychotic signification may retain the incomprehensibility of a private language destined never to be understood. Using Lacan's (over-quoted) belief that ‘the unconscious is structured like a language’, I show how his concept of ‘master signifiers’, when applied to the/my unconscious, read by metaphor and metonymy, is particularly helpful in understanding the apparently unintelligible ‘language’ of psychosis. Drawing on my own psychotic material, with reference to a specific ‘master signifier’ in one of my psychotic episodes, I also begin to explore the challenges that the solipsism of psychotic signification presents in the therapeutic relationship.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

It is a pleasure to announce the winning and commended papers in the 2016 Rozsika Parker Prize (p. 144), and to mark the distinctive place in the field that the BJP's competition, with its focus on creativity, has established. Benjamin Robinson's consideration of difficulty in the writing-up of clinical notes (Student Winner) and Sian Ellis's consideration of the translucent in supervision (Post-Qualification Winner) will be published in August this year; Ian Miller's consideration of Beckett in the context of psychoanalysis (Post-Qualification Commendation) will be published in November. Details of the 2017 competition are to be found on p. 278.

The second Clinical Commentary in our renewed, bi-annual series concerns a male patient ‘whose terror of growing up can provoke a profound sense of collapse from time to time’. This difficult and affecting material is both sensitively and at times challengingly explored by its three discussants.

The three papers in our core section, Clinical and Theoretical Practice, reflect the increasingly international reach of the BJP. Grazyna Czubinska (London) suggests that ‘the psychic work of emigration can be understood as a process of integrating splits between pre- and post-migration selves’ and, via discussion of a mutual enactment in a case history, that the analyst needs to allow herself to be a ‘real person’ in work with this patient group. Paula Collens and Francie Van Hout (Auckland, NZ) explore supervision as a ‘relational space where uncertainty and conflict can be born/e and given new meanings’, basing their paper on more than twenty years of work in higher education contexts. Dorit Lemberger (Ramat Gan, Israel), from a philosophical perspective, considers ‘the relationship between the role played by language in the constitution of the subject and how it functions in the process of communication between therapist and patient’. These are intricate papers, inviting careful reading and rereading.

The BJP is delighted to be publishing all the papers from last year's Freud Museum/Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis conference on Psychosis, in this issue and the next. Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz, who organized it with the Museum, places the day in the context of the many questions, theoretical and technical, that psychosis poses. Under the heading ‘History’, Haya Oakley offers a personal account of the anti-psychiatry movement, while Brian Martindale presents a comprehensive discussion of work with families where there is psychosis. Under the heading ‘Politics’, Jay Watts argues that ‘we do not and will not access the people who need our help most if we are precious about what a piece of work should look like’, while Barry Watt returns to ‘a key moment in the development of Kleinian psychoanalysis in post-war Britain’. In the next issue the papers address ‘Theory’ and ‘Technique’. As Bonnigal-Katz writes, the papers will inspire and enlighten, perhaps confuse, and move and disturb.

Elizabeth O'Loughlin

Elizabeth O'Loughlin

elizaariadne@blueyonder.co.uk

Elizabeth O'Loughlin  

My clinical practice is informed by the work of Jacques Lacan and as such my approach to the work has some fundamental differences from the clinical presentation of Mr B. There are some similarities in relation to issues of importance in the patient's speech, but radical differences in the way these issues are taken up in the therapy as a consequence of the differences in the position of the therapist. Rather than giving meaning and explanation to the patient's speech, I would take the effects of the unconscious as the ‘Royal Road’ to psychic truth. Effects that interrupt Mr B's speech such as slips of the tongue, bungled acts or bungled speech, dreams and so on as identified by Freud.

I want to start by taking up the question of diagnosis. Lacanian psychoanalysis puts special emphasis on the question of diagnosis. This does not mean pigeonholing the patient, but elaborating a framework which will help with the listening process and with attending to the particularity of each individual patient. There are markers first described by Freud, which distinguish the clinical structure, three in number, neurosis, psychosis and perversion. In practice, it isn't easy to make a differential diagnosis and the approach to each particular case, in the sense that each case is singular, demands a rigorous deciphering which may take some time.

PSYCHOSIS, FAMILIES, MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS, PSYCHOANALYSIS, RESEARCH, BLAME, PROJECTED GUILT, OPEN DIALOGUE

I offer some psychoanalytic perspectives and hypotheses to contribute to understanding why family interventions are rarely offered in psychosis. This is despite decades of evidence that family difficulties often predate onset of psychosis and that skilled family interventions are at least as effective as medication in reducing relapse rates. I contend that it is often unbearably disturbing for some families to even consider the possibility of having contributed to the vulnerability of a member to psychosis and that professionals fear accusations of ‘blaming’. Multisystem defences, involving both families and professionals, shift explanations for psychosis, reducing them as a disorder of brain chemistry and somewhat exclusively allowing the logical consequence that only pharmacological interventions ‘make sense’. I summarize the unfortunate consequences of these defences and suggest that there is denial of the important difference between describing possible family environmental contributing factors in psychosis and attributing ‘blame’. Whole team training that involves families and social networks in a highly respectful and humane manner overcomes some of these obstacles. Several decades of increasingly successful research in the Finnish psychodynamically orientated ‘need-adapted approach to psychosis’ resulting in recent more global interest in open dialogue indicate an effective way of engaging families and of achieving superior outcomes in returning individuals to social engagement as students or to employment.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

Regular readers will be aware that the publication of the ‘Essentially Ours, Specifically…’ papers on different theoretical orientations, across three issues of the BJP in 2014, was followed by Joe Schwartz's complementary collection on Attachment in May 2015. The publication of the Attachment papers was accompanied by an invitation to extend the series by developing other groups of papers in the same format: theoretical accounts of the model, that would then be illustrated by clinical material. In response, Alan Corbett approached the Journal, wondering if we might be interested in papers ‘looking at the birth and development of psychotherapy with patients with intellectual disabilities’, and proposing specific authors and topics. The Editorial Board and I welcomed this approach. He and I had an exchange about whether the theme of disability constituted an orientation (as such), or an approach to clinical phenomena. It was both, for him, as he said in an email: ‘It evolved as a response, but has at its heart a certain clinical approach that marks it out.’ Alan brought poise, discipline and commitment to this project throughout the eighteen months of its development, all the more remarkable given the illness he was suffering at the time. The ‘certain clinical approach that marks it out’ is precisely delineated in his editorial Introduction to the compelling papers by Valerie Sinason, Tamsin Cottis and Brett Kahr that follow. Very sadly, Alan Corbett died on 22 December 2016, while this issue of the Journal was in production; he did however see the proofs, a source of solace for those of us who knew him and knew how important the BJP project was to him. Brett Kahr's Appreciation of him will be published in our next issue.

I am grateful to Colin Campbell and Ann Horne for their editorial work on the disability psychotherapy papers.

Research - both formal and informal - is represented in the issue also. In the formal arena, Jan McGregor Hepburn is currently researching ‘the effects of being observed in infant observation’, using interviews with dyads of observers and observed. Noting that research hitherto has focused on the value of infant observation to trainee psychotherapists, McGregor Hepburn offers thought-provoking interim findings suggesting that themes of narcissism and projective identification provide a meaningful framework for interpreting the experience of the observed. Christopher Vincent and his colleagues report on their informal study of ‘the impact of recent technological innovations on their work as independent clinicians in private practice’. They look at those developments that had ‘crept up and become part of day-to-day practice almost without conscious awareness’ such as email and mobile phones; and then at technological innovations where psychotherapists ‘have exercised choice about whether and how to integrate them within their professional working lives’ such as social media, websites, VOIP and payments by bank transfer. This is a finely observed account, lending weight to the group's advocacy of more professional learning about new technology and its impact on the clinical.

PSYCHODYNAMIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, CHILD, CASE STUDY, INTERNALIZING BEHAVIOUR, ADJUSTMENT DISORDER

When psychopathology is considered as a developmental phenomenon, the data on child psychotherapy must be of interest to all therapists. The aim of this study was to assess the results of psychodynamic psychotherapy in a child with internalizing symptoms using data obtained from the patient, her mother, her teacher and her psychotherapist. A systematic single case study was performed. The data were obtained using the following tools: interviews, the Rorschach Method, the Child Behaviour Check List for Children and Adolescents, the Teachers Report Form and questionnaires completed by the patient's mother and therapist. The psychotherapeutic treatment lasted for 40 sessions and the patient was 8 years old at the start of therapy. She presented with head and stomach aches after the sudden death of her father, as well as difficulty adapting to her new school. The Rorschach results indicated improvement in cognitive triad variables, interpersonal relations and expressing affection. Data from the patient, mother and therapist converged to yield the clinical picture of a more spontaneous girl, dealing better with her feelings and more socially integrated. This points to the importance of using mixed methods to assess psychotherapies and of consulting multiple informants.

Liane Aukin 1936-2016

Kurt Ryz

Kurt Ryz

[k.ryz@talktalk.net]

Kurt Ryz  

I met Liane in the 1990s when we were both training with the Centre for Psychoanalytical Psychotherapy (CPP) in London. At the point when she began the training, she had already had a very full life, first as a stage and film actress, then as a radio producer and director, and finally as a writer, creating dramas for radio, television and the stage. For television her work included some of the early episodes of BBC TV's EastEnders, while for the theatre her play about the big-band leader, Ivy Benson, Silver Lady, was produced at the Birmingham Rep. She was highly respected as a director, and was especially influential in promoting women's theatre, as has been recognized with the establishment of a Liane Aukin archive in the Women's Theatre Collection at the University of Bristol.

After completing her training and the closure of the CPP, Liane applied to and was accepted by the London Centre for Psychotherapy (LCP), whereas I became a member of the British Association of Psychotherapists (BAP). We nevertheless stayed in touch and remained friends until the end. I was aware of her active involvement with the LCP and I think this was typical of the way in which she always fully engaged. She had regrets about the merger between the LCP, Lincoln Centre for Psychotherapy and BAP which she expressed to me, feeling deeply the loss both of the LCP, with its own distinctive identity, and of its building, which she admired.

Active involvement was always a trademark of Liane's personality and she made her contributions in a thoughtful but forthright manner. Being a writer she was able to apply her specialized skills to her therapeutic work, for example by running a writing workshop group for long-term and complex cases at the Willesden Centre for Psychotherapy, which she wrote about in an article called ‘Peeping out from behind the pages’ (Aukin, 2000). In this work she encouraged the innate creativity that she believed everyone owns, and was often moved by being witness to the difference that this work made to the group's participants. Her literary skills were also employed in her role as Book Reviews Editor for the BJP. She undertook this for five years, after four years as the representative of the CPP on the board of the Journal.

Jackie Gerrard

Jackie Gerrard

Jackie Gerrard  

I am writing these comments with thanks to the author who has submitted a most interesting article on her work and her thinking with her female patient. It seems fairly obvious that the therapist is a woman. When I read her first sentence, I found myself, as a Middle Group/Relational psychotherapist, thinking about Mervyn Glasser's core complex (1985), citing the difficulties in finding the right space in

450

relationships - and also about Balint's concepts of ocnophils and philobats (Balint, 1959). These ideas are borne out in her subsequent material.

Glasser postulates that within a relationship an infant has ‘intense longing for a condition of satiety and security achieved through fusion with the mother, a state which is expressed by the adult as a longing for ‘union’, ‘merging’, ‘at-one-ness’ (p. 408), but this fusion can lead to fears of complete annihilation. Then flight occurs and with it a sense of isolation and abandonment. The move in and out is repeated and a vicious circle occurs.

Balint (1959) makes a division between ocnophils, those who cling in relationships, and philobats who seek wide open spaces (Gerrard, 1994). In brief, the philobat is a person who relies on himself, who finds objects a nuisance or even a threat. In contrast, the ocnophil needs objects, cannot live without them and when in danger will cling to a firm and protective object, although alongside this is the constant fear that the object will let him down. It may drop him or even abandon him. His clinging is an expression of fear and also a defence against it. The ocnophil denies the independence of the object by clinging. He and the object are one - inseparable. His problem is, however, that by clinging he is not satisfying his original need - which was, in fact, to be held safely. Both ocnophils and philobats have reacted to the traumatic discovery of the separate existence of objects.

Maria is seen by the therapist as ‘totally psychically merged with her mother’ and then later ‘an intense transference relationship developed’. This is ocnophilic behaviour, but we see that during the therapy this begins to lessen as Maria struggles to be separate. She is moving towards philobatic behaviour during moments when she finds her therapist threatening. I have cited Balint elsewhere (Gerrard, 2000) stating that excessive interpretation in the transference can increase ocnophilic attachments.

Dorit Lemberger

Dorit Lemberger   Lecturer at Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel, in the Department of Hermeneutics and Cultural Studies, which includes a psychoanalysis and hermeneutics track. She is an advisor of many doctorate students who write interdisciplinary researches using Wittgenstein's philosophy and pragmatic thinkers to enlighten linguistic usage in psychoanalytic writings and practice. Her publications include Between Theology as Grammar and Religious Point of View in Wittgenstein Philosophy of Religion (2003), Experiencing the Meaning of a Word (2004), When Picture and Application Clash: The Paradox of Observation (2013), Variations of Metaphors: Wittgenstein's Contribution to Literary Studies (2015), Dialogical Grammar: Variations of Dialogue in Wittgenstein's Methodology (2015). ASPECT-SEEING, ASPECT-BLINDNESS, ASPECT'S ‘LIGHTING UP’, LANGUAGE-GAME, ‘I’ AS SUBJECT

The centrality of language in the psychoanalytic process has been recognized since Freud's time and is common to all schools of psychoanalysis. But despite the use of linguistic and literary terms such as ‘metaphor’ and ‘narrative’, the relationship between the role played by language in the constitution of the subject and how it functions in the process of communication between therapist and patient, in general and as a key to change, remains to be elucidated. Psychoanalysts such as Klein and Segal highlighted the importance of symbols in the constitution of the subject. However, they did not examine what actually takes place in linguistic acts, but their outcomes. I argue that in order to better understand the language-based processes we need to examine them from a linguistic perspective as this would demonstrate the neutrality of language and its diverse mechanisms. As a case study of the therapeutic process from the perspective of philology, this article examines the possibility of a change in treatment, inspired by variations on Wittgenstein's term ‘aspect’. Building on Wittgenstein's criticism of The Interpretation of Dreams, I propose expanding the use of this linguistic mechanism to include its function in the process of communication during therapy.

Sverre Varvin   Member and training and supervising analyst of the Norwegian Psychoanalytical Society and Professor at Oslo and Akershus University College of Applied Sciences. He has been president of the Norwegian Psychoanalytical Society and has held several positions at the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA) (vice president, board member, among others). He is currently chair of the IPA China Committee.

Hans Peter Søndergaard's comment [published in BJP 33(3) (2017) 418-21] on our article published in the November 2016 issue (Lesley & Varvin, 2016) appears to be a defence against what he believes is an attack on the very idea of dissociation and the idea that traumatic experience can cause dissociative reactions. It is largely concerned with his belief in the existence of the phenomenon of dissociation, especially of the personality - the existence of different identities alongside each other within a single person - and the efficacy of ‘trauma treatment’ based on dissociation theories. Alan Corbett 1963-2016

Brett Kahr

Brett Kahr

kahr14@aol.com

Brett Kahr  

On 22 December 2016, Dr Alan Corbett, a widely admired psychotherapist and pioneer of disability psychotherapy, died of cancer at the tragically young age of 53 years.

Born in London on 17 February 1963, Alan Corbett began his career in social work and, together with colleagues Tamsin Cottis and Stephen Morris, established a charity, Respond, in South London, in the early 1990s. Respond became the first organization in Great Britain devoted exclusively to the psychotherapeutic treatment of men and women struggling with disability, whether physical or intellectual.

For decades, many health professionals refused to believe that people with ‘mental handicap’ or ‘learning disabilities’ could benefit from the talking therapies. But inspired by the pioneering work of Valerie Sinason at the Tavistock Clinic, Corbett and his colleagues persevered in their efforts to speak intimately with patients who did not possess the linguistic functioning of most psychotherapy clients. Over the years, Corbett developed a sensitive capacity to make contact with brain-damaged people and with those who suffered from profound traumatization, which had rendered them unable to speak.

While working full-time at Respond, Alan Corbett embarked upon three trainings in order to improve his professional capabilities. First, he studied forensic psychotherapy at the Portman Clinic under the inspiring teaching of Dr Estela Welldon. Next, he undertook the training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy at the Guild of Psychotherapists. And ultimately, he completed his doctorate in clinical science under the supervision of Dr Georgia Lepper at the University of Kent.

Corbett's rich body of clinical experience allowed him to find an increasingly potent voice. He became a most accomplished writer, and in 1996, he and his colleagues published a book about their work with disabled patients, entitled Witnessing Nurturing Protesting: Therapeutic Responses to Sexual Abuse of People with Learning Disabilities (Corbett, Cottis & Morris, 1996).

I work primarily within a Kleinian object relations frame.

The therapist provides background information and detailed sessional material from work with Maria, a deeply troubled woman whose mother was sometimes ill with anxiety, whose father was asocial and autistic, and whose brother has both emotional and addiction problems. Already the scene is set for what is going to be a difficult therapy that is likely (and necessary) to be long and intensive if it is to be effective in promoting psychic change. My sense is that the therapy has got off to a good start and that Maria is fortunate to have found this particular therapist. However, although she has now been coming for at least a year, it is still early days and at this stage with such a patient I would not myself expect to have any more than several ideas about what the patient's presentation, and my experience of being with her in the room, mean with respect to her core difficulties.

One of the challenges with longer-term work is that we may have to sit with behaviours for a long time, sometimes for a very long time, without really understanding them and why the patient needs them. Such behaviours include leaving early, going to the toilet during sessions, leaving the door to the consulting room open, and many others. For Maria one such behaviour is arriving late. I think at this stage that we simply don't know why she needs to do it.

David Black  

Russell Meares, together with Robert Hobson, was one of the pioneers of the ‘conversational model’ of psychotherapy, which they worked on together in the 1960s when Meares, who is Australian, was doing his psychiatric training in London at the Maudsley and Royal Bethlem hospitals. Many readers of the BJP will remember Hobson (who went on to train at the SAP), a wonderfully warm, learned and witty speaker, who directed a therapeutic community at the Maudsley for 20 years and later became a central figure in psychotherapy in Manchester. He died in 1999. Meares too went on to a distinguished career in Australia; he is now Emeritus Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Sydney.

The conversational model is a psychotherapy approach focusing on self-experience, using ideas from many sources and echoing especially those of William James. Like Winnicott, it emphasized the experience of aliveness and well-being, and one original theoretical feature it stressed is the importance of ‘doubling’, the twofold awareness of how one is and how one seems to another - initially achieved by internalization of the ‘protoconversation’ (Trevarthen's term) between mother and preverbal infant. In health, the outcome is said to be the ‘stream of consciousness’ (James' term), seen as a positive freedom from arrests and fusions (transferences), and characterized by feelings of coherence, continuity, agency and so forth. ‘Conversation’ is the agent of relatedness; it is with an other who is perceived as a ‘fellow’ (as in ‘fellow-feeling’).

This practical and humane model, crudely described in my summary but worked out with great intellectual sophistication, was developed in response to the sort of patients Hobson saw at the Maudsley, deemed at the time ‘unanalysable’ and who would probably nowadays be diagnosed ‘borderline personality disorder’. The conversational model still exists, only slightly modified, under the name psychodynamic interpersonal therapy (PIT). It was well ahead of its time when Hobson invented it, and many of its ideas foresee those of today's intersubjective schools and of such approaches as mentalization therapy.

This impressive and compelling book explores the disturbance that can arise from sudden loss of the analytic relationship. We know that the analytic relationship invites a depth of connection which would be dangerous outside of the frame, and so when this unique container is abruptly removed, the bereaved patient risks losing parts of the self which were being lodged with the analyst. The subsequent transition to a new analyst, a ‘foster mother’, is a major task because what has been lost is irreplaceable. As one contributing author puts it: ‘The analyst and the analysand have created a world together, a culture of two, to which the rest of the world has little access’ (Young, p. 118).

The authors of this book are mostly drawn from North America, and each chapter reflects on a personal experience that caused the analytic frame to break or collapse.

Introduction

Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz

Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz

dbonnigk@btinternet.com

Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz  

Psychosis occupies a paradoxical place in psychoanalysis. A pivotal term in Freudian metapsychology, if not a paragon, it ranges across the full spectrum of the field, warranting a dynamic, topographical and economic discussion. Instrumental in Freud's elaboration of key concepts such as the unconscious or narcissism to name the most obvious ones, it is a goldmine for theoreticians. Yet, historically, it has struggled to find its place in psychoanalytic technique on account of the assumed ‘unanalysability’ of psychotic subjects. It is fair to say that in the absence of repression, of the kind of transference and resistance featured in the psychoanalytic treatment of neurosis, psychosis has always profoundly challenged the analytic method, leaving clinicians bereft of their common landmarks.

By blurring the basic partition between conscious and unconscious systems on the one hand, psychosis overturns the first topography. On the other hand, it radically stunts the second one, cutting it back from a triadic model (id/ego/superego) to a dyadic one: in psychosis, there is no triangulation to speak of. As for the link between subject and object, it is deeply disorganized to say the least, the impermanence of the object obstructing the advent of subjectivity. Is psychoanalysis relevant to the psychotic experience? Can it accommodate its evanescent subjects and the urgency of their ontological precariousness? Can it meet their rightful demand for subjective delineation and substantiality?

These questions - the place of psychoanalysis in psychosis, the place of psychosis in psychoanalysis - brought together an outstanding panel of clinicians in March 2016, under the auspices of the Freud Museum, London. The answers that were given across a variety of theoretical perspectives (Lacanian, Kleinian, systemic, relational and attachment theory, among others) were fertile and hopeful, despite the political and economic difficulties besetting the psychoanalytic treatment of psychosis. I am deeply grateful to the Freud Museum - Ivan Ward and Stefan Marianski, especially -for the opportunity to organize this conference and for their trust and generosity. The conference was a fundraiser for the Psychosis Therapy Project, the psychoanalytic project I launched at Islington Mind in 2013, thanks to the kindness of Peter Nevins and all the wonderful staff at Islington Mind - Tom Fea and Pat O'Driscoll, especially. The Psychosis Therapy Project is a clinical project committed to the implementation, the development and the transmission of a distinct technique.

Alan Corbett

Alan Corbett

Alan Corbett   DClinSci FIPD was a UKCP registered psychoanalytic psychotherapist, and a member of the Training Committee of the Guild of Psychotherapists. He was the editor of the Institute of Psychotherapy and Disability Monograph Series, and the author of Disabling Perversions: Forensic Psychotherapy with People with Intellectual Disabilities (2014) and of Psychotherapy with Male Survivors of Sexual Abuse (2016). He had been Clinical Director of Respond, Immigrant Counselling and Psychotherapy (ICAP), and the CARI Foundation. He taught on a number of psychoanalytic trainings in Britain and Ireland, lectured internationally and published widely on disability, psychotherapy and trauma. Address for correspondence c/o Brett Kahr: [kahr14@aol.com]

Intellectual disability is an intersubjective phenomenon. The troublesome, confusing weight of a cognitive deficit comes into sharpest relief within the confines of a relationship. ‘A’, who has an intellectual disability, seeks to communicate with ‘B’, who does not. The success of the communication is not dependent on A's relatively low IQ, his problems with retaining memory or his struggle to form a narrative. For the communication to have meaning relies largely on B's capacity to recognize the limits of A's verbal skills, and to take active steps to compensate for them. If B does not recognize the disability, or is simply uninterested in it, the communication will falter and A will feel even more disabled and misunderstood than before. If B thinks carefully about, for example, the number of syllables A can bear a word to have, A may end the conversation feeling heard and less disabled.

In collating three papers to illustrate the use of psychoanalytic psychotherapy with patients with disabilities, I approached three practitioners whose long clinical histories encompass the salient points of disability psychotherapy. Disability psychotherapy refers to psychotherapy where the patient has a recognized disability and the therapist takes active steps to ensure that the disability does not prevent something therapeutic from happening. A question I sought to explore in approaching this journal concerned specialism and niche. In creating a term to describe this work, are we implying or declaring that it lies outside the parameters of conventional psychotherapy? My hope is that each paper describes a psychotherapeutic process that has notable diversions from the mainstream but that still belongs within it. Valerie Sinason's paper introduces the concept of an analytic boundary that can breathe - a far cry from the notion of a static frame that constricts rather than allows therapeutic movement. The insecurity that underpins an overly rigid boundary may be thought about, in the context of disability psychotherapy, as an intersubjective failure, denoting a lack of capacity on the part of the therapist to consider, in counter-transferential terms, the impact of the patient's disability not only on the therapy, but on the therapist. Tamsin Cottis's paper considers this question from the perspective of work with children with intellectual disabilities - a discipline that illustrates vividly the need for the therapist to deal with attacks upon the boundary with resilience and, crucially, creativity. Brett Kahr's paper places the reader at the heart of a clinical encounter for which few clinical trainings will have prepared us. The resilience demonstrated by all these authors in their responses to their patients demonstrates some of the qualities needed to work with this patient group.

All psychotherapy is dependent on a frame, a structure. We require boundaries in order to feel and provide containment. However, when working with patient groups who have been excluded from mainstream risk-averse treatment we learn more about the nature of professional boundaries. A boundary needs to be nurtured and thought about. It needs to breathe and to come from thought. A rigid boundary is a different matter. Where is the humble concept of not knowing? What makes flexible guidelines become rigidified into inflexible codes and barriers? In interrogating techniques that do not work with people with intellectual disabilities we learn more about shared areas of social disability. This paper focuses on questions of analytic neutrality, affect, anger, transparency, and disability psychotherapy in the external as well as internal world.

The supervisory relationship is complex and multi-layered, given the multiple sources of unconscious dynamics between patient, supervisee and supervisor. The concept of the parallel process has brought greater depth and understanding to the supervisor's countertransference as reflective of the dynamics within the analytic relationship. The tendency, however, is to consider the parallel process as occurring in one direction only: from the analytic relationship into the supervisory one. In this paper, I consider the multidirectional movement of transference and countertransference between both relationships, including where the supervisor might be the point of origin, rather than the recipient. Clinical material from two patients brought to supervision is analysed from four different vertices: the parallel process; the developmental aspects of the supervisory relationship and of the supervisee; my own potential transferences onto the supervisee and/or the patient; and the potential effect of my transference onto the supervisee, the patient and their interaction. I also refer to some paintings by Richard Diebenkorn, as these offer a powerful metaphor for understanding the challenges in supervision of creating a secure frame, while also allowing for a more ‘translucent’ space, within which the multi-layered dimensions can be imagined and become capable of continual transformation.

MEMORY, TIME, TIMELESSNESS, AUTISTIC SPECTRUM DISORDER, FRAGMENTATION, PRIMITIVE MENTAL STATES

Deciphering the way patients experience time provides an additional key to primitive mental areas which do not express themselves in the usual verbal or symbolic ways and can help us and our patients better understand these deep layers of the psyche. It is when the issue of time moves to the centre of experience as a separate and predominant aspect of existence, that there and then occurs a disturbance in our continuous and natural transition between various temporalities, one that often exposes an inner rupture, many times of a very early origin. The paper first focuses on a number of art works which portray attempts to deal with death anxiety by capturing the moment, or watching, controlling, organizing, cataloguing the movement of time as though such attempts could freeze time and make it endlessly prolongued. Second, theoretical aspects and clinical vignettes focus on understanding the experience of time as fractured and fragmented; on experiences of timelessness, and, on stereotypical, ritualistic, autistic-like relations to time, perceived as frozen still. In addition, conceptualizing the analyst/writer's experience of time in the presence of her patients provided a unique tool for expanding the understanding of the patients' internal world.
