THE UNCONSCIOUS, THE ID, THE OTHER, SEDUCTION, TRANSLATION, THE DRIVE

This paper is an attempt to present Jean Laplanche's interpretation of the Freudian field as one that is driven and shaped by opposing gravitational pulls. These he represents by developing Freud's analogy of the Copernican and psychoanalytic revolutions to demonstrate the successive decentrings and recentrings of the human subject in relation to a primal and formative other at the level of a psychoanalytic theory that is itself alternately both ‘Copernican’ and ‘Ptolemaic’. In doing so, he replicates those movements at work at the level of the formation of human subjectivity. Focusing on Freud's shifting conceptions of the unconscious, the drive and the id, this paper seeks to show how Laplanche radicalizes certain ‘Copernican’ elements of Freud's metapsychology to establish the primacy of the other and the dimension of ‘primal seduction’ in concepts intended by Freud to decentre the narcissistic illusions of the ego, but which are captured by regressive movements of thought, retreating to ‘Ptolemaic’ conceptions of an endogenous, biologically grounded development of subjectivity.

Nathan Szajnberg MD

Nathan Szajnberg

[nmoshe@gmail.com]

Nathan Szajnberg   Received undergraduate and medical degrees at the University of Chicago in 1974. He studied with Bruno Bettelheim (about whom he edited a book, Educating the Emotions), Peter Giovacchini, Alfred Flarsheim and Roy Grinker, among others, in Chicago. He completed his psychoanalytic studies at the St Louis Psychoanalytic Institute. He has been the Wallerstein Research Fellow in Psychoanalysis (2005-16), Freud Professor at the Hebrew University (2007-10), and the Ticho Lecturer. He has written three books on development: Lives Across Time (with Henry Massie); Reluctant Warriors: Israelis Suspended Between Rome and Jerusalem; and Sheba and Solomon's Return: Ethiopian Children in Israel. His novel, JerusaLand, will be published this year and he is completing a book on father-son relations based on the Biblical Jacob-Joseph story.
WINNICOTT, PIGGLE, ENIGMA, ANALYST-PATIENT RELATIONSHIP, CHILD ANALYSIS

The Piggle, in its 40th anniversary year, was published after Winnicott's death. He treated this 2-year 4-month-old girl over two and a half years. Yet, until recently, The Piggle has been ambivalently reviewed and minimally studied, despite elegant posthumous papers, a recent introduction to Winnicott's collected works and an interview with the ‘Piggle’ in adulthood. We show that Winnicott's technique and interpretations fall into three categories: (1) early Kleinian ‘deep’ interpretations; (2) an Anna Freudian approach with developmental considerations, respect for defences, the analyst as a new developmental object; (3) a Winnicottian attitude and interpretations that hew close to the manifest material and emphasize the environment-individual relationship and full-bodied play. Winnicott's ‘interpretations’ include verbal interpretation, prosody, gesture, facial expression, body movements and contact. Winnicott details the child's reactions to the different interpretations. We close suggesting that Winnicott carried on dialogues, not only with the child, but also internal dialogues with former teachers (Klein/Riviere; Strachey as his first analyst and so connecting to the Freudians in the Institute of Psychoanalysis) and perhaps with Anna Freud as a colleague after her arrival in London in 1938. This is a manifestation of false versus true (analytic) selves. Understanding Winnicott's internal struggle with his former teachers/analysts, corrected by his responsiveness to the child's responses and suggestions, resulted in his bringing a truer self to this child's treatment and unravels The Piggle's enigmatic qualities.

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley

hayaoakley@blueyonder.co.uk

Haya Oakley   Born and educated in Israel where she worked as a psychiatric social worker in a mental hospital. She has been practising psychoanalysis in London since 1968. After a brief spell at the David Cooper ‘anti-university’ group she joined the Philadelphia Association where she worked for many years with R.D. Laing and colleagues training psychotherapists and working in therapeutic households. In 1997 she left the Philadelphia Association and set up, with others, the Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis. She has been a member of the Guild of Psychotherapists since 1982 and is a founder member of the College of Psychoanalysts UK. She is Honorary Fellow of UKCP where she served as chair of the Psychoanalytic Section, 1993-96. Her interests include psychoanalysis and psychosis, the politics of psychotherapeutic organizations, issues surrounding attempted regulation of the ‘impossible profession’, and the comparative study of psychoanalytic theories. She is involved in teaching, supervising and analysing trainees, and has contributed to a number of publications as well as TV and radio programmes.
ANTI-PSYCHIATRY, COOPER, LAING, PHILADELPHIA ASSOCIATION, SCHIZOPHRENIA, MADNESS AND CIVILIZATION

This is a personal account of life in the Philadelphia Association from the late 1960s to the 1990s when some of the ideas of Basaglia, Cooper, Deleuze, Esterson, Fanon, Foucault, Guattari, Laing and Szasz were put into practice. Cooper's Psychiatry and Anti-psychiatry (1967) was the inspiration for what appeared as an international movement within psychiatry, influenced, among other things, by Foucault's Madness and Civilization (1967). Szasz believed mental illness to be a myth created by society; Cooper believed that the family was an instrument of oppression perpetrating psychological violence on its members; Laing believed that if one studied the specific forms of communication within families of schizophrenics one could make madness intelligible and therefore amenable to some form of psychotherapy. The paper highlights the evolving understanding of psychosis within the Philadelphia Association and the relationship of psychosis to psychoanalysis. It suggests that far from being a misguided blip in the history of psychiatry, ‘anti-psychiatry’ could be seen as having revolutionized our discourse in relation to psychosis in a way which has left a worthy and lasting legacy, linking treatment to how we treat one another.

ONLINE THERAPY, ONLINE COUNSELLING, INTERNET THERAPY, PSYCHOTHERAPY, TECHNOLOGY, THERAPEUTIC FRAME, COMMUNICATION, TELEANALYSIS

This paper is a report on an informal study by a small group of psychotherapists interested in exploring the impact of recent technological innovations on their work as independent clinicians in private practice. The range of technologies studied included websites, email, mobile phones, and internet-based banking services for payment and receipt of fees. Some of the group had experience of using internet-based video software (or Voice Over Internet Protocol/VOIP software) for providing therapy and/or establishing supervisory and training links. The study found that these technologies have had both positive and negative impacts on professional practice and, in particular, records how practitioners have managed these changes within their clinical practice. The study notes the lack of professional training about these matters and highlights some of the issues that need to be addressed in redressing this situation.

‘Janet vs Freud’ on Traumatization: A Critique of the Theory of Structural Dissociation from an Object Relations Perspective

Hans Søndergaard

Hans Søndergaard

Kris- och traumacentrum, Wollmar Yxkullsgatan 25, 118 50 Stockholm, Sweden hps@live.se; hans.peter.sondergaard@ki.se

Hans Søndergaard   Psychiatrist, psychotherapist, and associate professor at Kris- och traumacentrum (Center for Crisis and Trauma) in Stockholm. He has worked with refugees and other traumatized clients, written several book chapters in Swedish on post-traumatic stress disorder, and participated in training in transcultural psychiatry for doctors and other specialists.

In ‘“Janet vs Freud” on traumatization: A critique of the theory of structural dissociation from an object relations perspective’ [BJP 32(4) (2016) 436-55], Joan Lesley and Sverre Varvin express concern that the theory of structural dissociation of the personality has taken hold in Norway, and has caused undue and unnecessary confusion regarding treatment of clients with dissociative disorders. According to the authors there is no need to change treatment models for subjects with dissociative disorders who might well be treated with psychoanalytic methods.

Lesley and Varvin first offer a summary of the theory of structural dissociation of the personality. Next they criticize this theory and its practice. Finally they present two cases that in their view had been wrongly treated using ideas of the theory and practice they criticize, but that fared well following psychoanalytic treatment based on object relations theory.

While their recapitulation of the theory of structural dissociation is quite comprehensive in some regards, it also entails several misunderstandings. For example, the theory is not mechanistic as Lesley and Varvin state. Further, there is a lack of a deeper appreciation of the implications of the theory of structural dissociation (see below for detailed comments). Lesley and Varvin cite Etzel Cardeña, a well respected researcher for his criticism that it is hard to conceive of trauma as a division of the personality. Further they cite Paul Dell for other critical remarks, thus finding ammunition for their criticism, from within the field, so to speak. However, while Cardeña and Dell criticize the definition of structural dissociation of the personality, they do not seem to question the theory and the existence of dissociation of the personality in trauma as such.

An important aspect of the current interest in dissociative disorders in Norway is an interest in psychological trauma in part for historical reasons. There is the groundbreaking research of Leo Eitinger on concentration camp survivors, long before the notion of post-traumatic stress disorder.

Alberto Stefana

Alberto Stefana

Alberto Stefana   Adult, adolescent and child psychotherapist. He currently works at the Psychiatric Unit of the Spedali Civili Hospital of Brescia (Italy) and in private practice. He is interested in issues of clinical theory and technique, history and epistemology of psychoanalysis, and the relationship between psychoanalysis and the other sciences. His book, History of Countertransference: From Freud to the British Object Relations School, was published this year (Routledge, 2017).
EROTIC TRANSFERENCE, EROTIC COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, IDEALIZATION, EROTIZATION, SEXUALIZATION

This article presents some reflections on the delicate and complex phenomenon of erotic transference (and of correlated countertransference issues), a particular form of transference that compels the subject to convert the object into an erotic phantasy. It must be noted that the adjective ‘erotic’ is a bridge concept between ‘pleasurable’ and ‘sexual’. It follows that erotic transference can have various tonalities that range from loving to sexualized and from a dream state (benign) to a drugged or delusional state (malignant). Some writers distinguish between various types of erotic transference, which, however, can be placed on the ‘pleasurable↔sexual’ continuum, and which can in turn be superimposed onto the ‘preoedipal↔oedipal’ dimension.

Stijn Vanheule PHD

Stijn Vanheule

stijn.vanheule@ugent.be

Stijn Vanheule   Clinical psychologist and a professor of psychoanalysis and clinical psychological assessment at Ghent University, Belgium, where he is Chair of the Department of Psychoanalysis. He is also a psychoanalyst in private practice (Member of the New Lacanian School) and the author of numerous journal articles and books, including The Subject of Psychosis - A Lacanian Perspective and Psychiatric Diagnosis Revisited: From DSM to Clinical Case Formulation.
LACAN, PSYCHOSIS, MANIA, TRANSFERENCE, UNCONSCIOUS, MANIC DEPRESSION

Starting from the hypothesis that psychosis makes up a structure with a precise status for the unconscious, the author explores how, from a Lacanian point of view, the treatment of psychosis is organized. Special attention is paid to the specificity of the psychotic symptom and the way transference characteristically takes shape. It is indicated that the occurrence of psychotic symptoms bears witness to a subjective crisis, in which no signifiers provide support when, at the level of the unconscious, the subject is dealing with fundamental self-directed epistemic questions (‘who am I?’) and questions concerning the intentionality of the other (‘what do you want?’). Characteristically, such questions are organized around intimate topics like dealing with parenthood and authority; life in the light of death; sexuality in relation to love and procreation; and sexual identity. Psychotic crises are triggered upon confrontations with such issues in daily life, while no support by means of a master signifier or Name-of-the-Father can be found. Crucial to the Lacanian approach to treatment is that the psychoanalyst aims at restoring a place for the subject in relation to the Other, which is threatened in episodes of acute psychosis. Clinical material from Lacanian work with a female patient suffering from manic-depressive psychosis is discussed.

ALVAREZ, ATTACHMENT, CHILD PSYCHOTHERAPY, DISABILITY, OBJECT GAMES, SINASON, TRANSITIONAL OBJECT, TRAUMA

This paper will consider what impact a learning disability may have on development and transition in a child's life. With reference to Hollins and Sinason's ‘Three secrets’ (2000), Alvarez's ‘Levels of psychoanalytic work’ (2012), and attachment theory, I will reflect on the development of the self when there is learning disability. The paper will go on to relate Winnicott's paper, ‘Transitional objects and transitional phenomena’ (1953) to the theory and practice of integrative arts child psychotherapy (IACP). In IACP, objects, play and creativity form a central part of the treatment. Drawing on clinical material from my long-term treatment of two young people in particular, I will link the therapeutic effect of objects with Winnicott's ideas about creativity, aggression, motivation and the expression of self. In the paper I set out how, through the therapeutic use of objects and what I call, ‘object games’ we were able to address the children's experiences of trauma as well as the impact of their disabilities. I will describe the changes I saw in the internal worlds of my patients which in turn led to significant and positive changes in their relationships with self and with others. These changes came, over time, to allow them greater independence and self-determination in everyday life.

DAVID HUME, JOHN LOCKE, FRANZ BRENTANO, EMPIRICISM, ASSOCIATIONIST PSYCHOLOGY, CAUSATION, AGENCY, DECISION-MAKING

In Freud's representations of the origins of psychoanalysis he tended to deny the existence of any significant philosophical or literary precursors, preferring to present psychoanalysis as an empirical science. This paper will situate Freud's work in the context of the philosophical crisis resulting from David Hume's pushing of empiricism to its limits. The difficulties that Hume encountered in his attempt to observe the observer raised unsettling questions concerning the constitution of the psyche and its implications for the possibility of knowledge and agency that a succession of subsequent thinkers struggled to answer. Freud's work can fruitfully be seen as an intervention in this debate, which, as we shall see, is still ongoing.

Richard Tan

Richard Tan

richard@richard41.plus.com

Richard Tan  

Holding in mind Susan Isaacs' statement that “Phantasy is the primary content of unconscious mental processes” (1949, p. 82), I shall start with my impression about the work in general and then move on to more specific thoughts and experience of the session presented. This is an interesting but complex case. My commentary takes the form of freely associating to the material provided.

First, I expected the clinical material to be more detailed. It was in fact rather short and I found myself floundering and not being able to settle down to thinking in a more focused way. I was rather surprised at the lack of the patient's developmental history in the material. Perhaps this was due to the need to preserve confidentiality, which was perfectly understandable, but might be overly cautious, suggesting a degree of anxiety of being seen/known. It seems there was something secretively child-like about this and the exchanges in the session felt intellectual and explanatory.

The clinical material suggests the presence of an overwhelmingly frightened child in the man. The patient's parents are Holocaust survivors and struggling with its aftermath perhaps in the form of a tense depressive family atmosphere suggested in the history. I think the patient is struggling with this too in the form of his internalized objects. We know that a frightened child is also an angry child, and it is this anger that the therapist is struggling to bring to the surface. My impression is that the patient is somewhat stuck in early latency, with intellectualization as a defence against his emotions. It reminds me of Meltzer's young patient who knows everything about Freud but nothing about sex; he is clever and intelligent but struggling with being human and its accompanying flaws in being so.

Hanoch Yerushalmi PHD

Hanoch Yerushalmi

hyerush1@univ.haifa.ac.il

Hanoch Yerushalmi   Clinical Psychologist and serves as associate professor and chair of the Department of Community Mental Health at the University of Haifa, Israel. He has formerly been the Director of the Student Counseling Center at the Hebrew University in Israel. He has published numerous articles on relational psychoanalytic therapy, supervision and psychiatric rehabilitation.
REGRESSIVE, PROGRESSIVE, DEVELOPMENTAL THRUSTS, META-COMMUNICATION, INTERSUBJECTIVE

This article examines the basic dynamics underlying some of the spontaneous developmental changes created out of the unique structure of analytic therapy. These dynamics include two types of basic forces working in the therapeutic setting: regressive and progressive urges and thrusts, which set opposite processes in motion. The progressive forces, highlighted in the article, are derived from developmental pressures. These forces create the conditions for people to seek new ways of experiencing the self and of connecting to significant others in what they sense to be a more mature and authentic manner. The literature describes how, through the healing power of therapeutic transference and regressive states, therapy can help to release obstructions to these developmental thrusts, which are created by childhood traumas caused by care takers. In this article, however, the release of obstructions is examined through meta-communication, an analytic clinical intervention that can enhance expression and realization of patients' progressive wishes.

This clinical roundtable features a presentation by Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz who posits the impairment of the mechanisms of repression as characteristic of psychosis and discusses its consequences for the analyst, especially as regards the place of interpretation. She shows how the analyst's encounter with the psychotic experience radically challenges and paradoxically validates psychoanalytic technique. In response to Bonnigal-Katz's discussion, Tomasz Fortuna offers an overview of the psychoanalytic tradition's response to psychosis, raising the issue of the relation between psychosis and neurosis. Christos Tombras, on the other hand, invokes Freud's discussion of Schreber's Memoirs from a Lacanian perspective and addresses the question of language and experience.

SUPERVISION, GROUPS/ORGANIZATIONS, RELATIONAL CONFLICT, COMPLEMENTARITY, LEARNING, PARALLEL PROCESS, CLINICAL RHOMBUS, TRAINING ORGANIZATIONS

At the site of interpersonal conflict resides the potential for learning. This paper presents psychodynamic theories, empirical research and a fictional case study of psychotherapy group supervision. Supervision is discussed in terms of teaching and learning, triangular relations, and group and organizational perspectives. We examine the interconnectedness of patterns of distress that emerge within dynamic relational systems at the levels of the macro-social, organizational, group and individual. The concepts of equivalence, parallel process and reflection process provide frameworks for this discussion. We explore the constraints and dynamic influence of the organization upon the supervision relationship and the ethical tensions that construct im/possible positions for the supervisor. The case study tells a fictional story of a supervision group situated in an organizational context - a university psychotherapy education programme. A collapse of the group into complementarity, that is into polarized conflicted positions, proffers a vitalizing opportunity for learning. Through the clinical discussion, we reveal how this is contingent on the group's capacity to think together about the meaning of their struggle and to transcend a binary conflict and achieve ‘the third’.

ATTACHMENT THEORY, PSYCHOSIS, SCHIZOPHRENIA, PSYCHIATRY, TRAUMA, DISSOCIATION

This paper examines how attachment theory has informed understanding of psychosis and has the potential to improve practice working with those who have accrued a diagnosis of psychosis. The treatment of psychosis is placed in its historical context, and commentary is made about the current treatments of those with psychosis and possible future developments. A psychoanalytic perspective is explored, and concern about the apparent colonization of the social and psychological by the biological expressed. Differing understanding and explanations of psychotic symptoms are explored and the predominance of biological explanations of the aetiology of psychosis is questioned. A brief description of attachment theory is given, before concluding how attachment theory informs understanding of psychosis and the implications for treatment.

SESSION, WRITE-UP, NOTES, SUPERVISION, METAPHOR, TRAINEE EXPERIENCE, AESTHETICS, SESSION BLOCK, THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP

Writing up session notes is essential to therapists' practice, yet the literature on psychotherapeutic writing focuses almost exclusively on more complex tasks, such as preparing case studies or pieces for publication. Nonetheless, problems with writing up seem widespread: this article finds that 85% of trainees report difficulty. Such ‘session block’ has not before been defined. Given the absence of well-accepted psychotherapeutic tools to overcome such block, and given that writing sessions is a challenge of representation - a phenomenon well described in the world of art - this article appropriates methods from aesthetic theory to address the problem. Applying first the Classical aesthetic metaphor of art-as-mirror, the pressure on therapists to produce a clear likeness of the session is explored, and the mirror metaphor is found to be as oppressive as it is widely accepted. By contrast, a revolutionary metaphor from the Romantic era, namely art-as-lamp, wherein the poet casts an inner creative light over the world, holds promise in overcoming countertransferential blocks and permitting an imaginative write-up. This too, though, has drawbacks, and the article concludes by proposing a method which, by integrating metaphors, permits a free-flowing write-up of the session, both creatively rich and clinically accurate.

MIGRATION, CRISIS, TRAUMA, INTERSUBJECTIVITY, PSYCHOANALYSIS, IDENTITY, LANGUAGE, CULTURE

The author addresses some issues regarding patients who relocate and who struggle with adaptation to a new reality. She argues that emigration is a complex psychological phenomenon that requires a therapist to pay special attention to the issue of language, difference and identity, and suggests that the issues of different culture and language in analytic psychotherapy need to be considered as part of a wider cultural context to which we all belong, rather than a specialized area of interest. The paper illustrates, through the clinical example of an East European male patient, that the psychic work of emigration can be understood as a process of integrating splits between pre- and post-migration selves. The author concludes that the analyst needs to let herself be involved as a ‘real person’ to reach the non-interpretative aspects of the patient's psyche through a mutuality of shared experience to promote a change.

Jan Hepburn

Jan Hepburn   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice in Northumberland. She is the Registrar of the British Psychoanalytic Council and on the Training Committee of the North of England Training in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, where she has also been an infant observation tutor. She is in the process of a doctoral study at the University of Northumbria into the effects of being observed in infant observation. Address for correspondence: [janhep@gmail.com]
PRIMARY NARCISSISM, PROJECTION, PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATION, INFANT OBSERVATION, RESEARCH

Esther Bick introduced psychoanalytic infant observation courses at the Tavistock Clinic in London in 1948 as part of the training for child psychotherapists in order to facilitate clinical training. She thought that being able to observe infantile processes as they developed was a good grounding for psychoanalytic practice, and noted that it was helpful for mothers to have someone visiting who could admire and appreciate their baby. Since then, there has been considerable writing and some research about the value of infant observation to trainee psychotherapists (Sternberg, 2005), but relatively little has been written about the effect of being observed in this way. Watillon-Naveau (2008) wrote about the families she visited after they had been observed; Bekos (2006) did an MA study of three observed mothers. Both concluded that it was an important experience for the observed. This paper endeavours to understand more about what exactly can be perceived in the interrelated and intersubjective communication and feedback loops between the infant, their primary carers and the observer. The author argues for the theoretical possibility of healthy narcissism and for projective identification being a reactive process. The paper considers what learning from infant observation can offer psychoanalytic theory and what clinical implications could be drawn.

We are delighted to present the second Clinical Commentary of this new series, and are grateful to the psychotherapist who has offered clinical material and to the three commentators.

Clinical Material

Mr B, a single man in his late 30s, has been in twice weekly psychotherapy with me for several years.

In the early days of treatment, he was not able to develop relationships or any independent life of his own. He had no experience of any sexual relationships and his emotional immaturity was striking. Although intellectually clever, Mr B was unable to complete his postgraduate university studies, had never worked, even in a casual or holiday job, and spent a lot of his time at home. One of four siblings, he continued to live at home, still went on holidays with family members and described his extended family as almost the only other people he had social contact with. His presenting problem in starting therapy was that he was unable to complete his postgraduate degree following a number of extensions. It became clear early on that the significance of being unable to finish his studies was that he would then have to start to live his life as an adult - finding a job, possibly leaving home, starting to develop adult relationships - all of which terrified him at the time.

He has now completed his studies and, after considerable delay and difficulty, has found work in a professional capacity in a large company. He comes from a family with a complex Holocaust background and this plays a pivotal role in his sense of guilt, delayed ability to take ownership of his own aggression and liveliness, and his development as an adult potent man. He experiences great difficulty moving on from ‘the Holocaust’, both in his family's tragic experience of it, and also as an internal persecutory object which he continually re-evokes, especially during times when he is making some progress in his life.

These days, there is an increasing sense of awareness in him of time going by as he gets older, and how this involves separation, endings and the possibility of new beginnings.

PSYCHOSIS, PSYCHOANALYTIC THERAPY, ENGAGEMENT, OPEN DIALOGUE, TEAMS

Psychoanalytic work can help people meaningfully engage with aspects of psychotic experience which feel overwhelming. However, such contact is only possible if we offer a practice that is acceptable to both potential patients, and the family, team and social groups they exist within. As a psychoanalytic community we are failing to do this, partly because of the political terrain, but also due to our perceived unapproachability. I argue that the type of tentative, humble positions advocated by approaches such as ‘open dialogue’ allows psychoanalytic techniques to be more palatable to those experiencing psychosis. This is especially important given how language functions in psychosis, and the histories of intrusion and oppression that language interacts with. Clinical material from work with a female patient suffering from paralysing visual hallucinations is discussed, with a particular emphasis on how contact was only possible once certain discourse knots were deconstructed. Such work requires giving up some traditional ideas around technique in the interest of serving one of the most disenfranchised client groups.

Barry Watt   Member of the Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis, a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice and a senior psychotherapist at the Psychosis Therapy Project at Mind, Islington. PSYCHOSIS, TECHNIQUE, MELANIE KLEIN, HANNA SEGAL, HISTORY OF BRITISH PSYCHOANALYSIS

This paper undertakes a return to a key moment in the development of Kleinian psychoanalysis in post-war Britain, focusing on the Kleinian clinic of psychosis during the period. Through a reconsideration of a seminal paper by Hanna Segal, it seeks to address the following question: given the originality of Klein and her colleagues at that time, why did they adopt such a rigid approach to innovation in the clinical treatment, if not the theorization, of the psychoses? By focusing on some of the ways in which extra-clinical factors, especially the institutional politics from within which the Kleinian clinical orientation was forged, this paper hopes to contribute to a broader understanding of certain factors influencing the emergence of distinctive theoretical and clinical cultures. Making use of insights from philosopher of science Ian Hacking in conjunction with Segal's own notion of ‘symbolic equations’, it is argued that there is a ‘symbolic equation’ in the Kleinian failure, at the time, to metaphorize or interpret Freud's technical prescriptions for psychoanalysis, resulting in a symbolic equation between their clinical technique and the hypothesized symbolic equations of their patients.

I recommend this enjoyable book not only to mental health professionals but also to anyone interested in the nature of madness. It addresses a gap in the market where

269

there is very little accessible literature applying psychoanalytic ideas to frontline experience.

Marcus Evans has a great deal of experience in mental health. He qualified as a nurse in 1983 and over time developed a strong conviction about the importance of psychoanalytic understanding. In recent years he has been working at the Tavistock Clinic, becoming both the Head of Nursing and the Associate Clinical Director of the Adult Department. He currently works psychodynamically with some of the most challenging patients treated in the NHS.

In his book Evans talks with authenticity about working, supervising and consulting to frontline services in mental health. He clearly understands the intense level of disturbance, complexity and pressure that clinicians have to cope with in the current health service, with an ever-increasing demand to provide a high standard of care for a growing number of seriously disturbed patients, and reducing resources.

The book's main theme is the difficulty working within this heart of madness - that sanity is fragile and the health professional can easily get lost in mania and the wish to rescue patients.

Evans shows that the historical split between psychiatry and psychoanalysis is unhelpful. Throughout the book he uses material from his work over the years to illustrate the value of applying psychoanalytic ideas to psychiatric work:

… in the treatment of ill patients psychiatry needs psychotherapy, and psychoanalytic psychotherapy needs psychiatry. When they work well together they act as the parents of the clinical setting with the listening approach of psychotherapy complementing the objective and scientific approach of psychiatry. (p. 203)

In the introduction, Evans emphasizes that a psychoanalytic understanding can help us to see the powerful unconscious dynamics that underlie all mental health difficulties. He draws on psychoanalytic theory and the work of colleagues such as Lucas and Sohn, who have supported him over the years, to describe a model of the mind where different parts of the personality are in a dynamic relationship with each other. There are healthy constructive ‘non-psychotic’ parts that are in touch with reality and there are destructive ‘psychotic’ parts that use omnipotent and primitive defences such as projection, rationalization and denial, to remain out of touch with reality. Evans believes that psychotic thinking and structures lie underneath most neurotic conditions (p. 3). When an individual has a mental illness the psychotic part of their personality has dominance over the non-psychotic part, which is still present but may be hidden. The challenge for mental health professionals is to find and support the non-psychotic part of the personality. He uses the example of the Mental Health Tribunal as a place where these two parts of the personality may be seen in daily practice: ‘Although the psychotic part of the patient's mind might argue against the section, the sane part of his mind can feel reassured that the mental health system understands the extent of the problem’ (p. 58).

Tomasz Fortuna

Tomasz Fortuna

tfortuna@tavi-port.nhs.uk

He is a member of the British Psychoanalytical Society, Hanna Segal Institute for Psychoanalytic Studies and the scientific committees of both organizations. I must play their game, of not seeing I see the game.

(R.D. Laing, 1971, p. 1)

Although Sigmund Freud wrote extensively about the unconscious meanings underlying manifest symptoms, behaviours and speech, he remained sceptical about the possibility of treating people suffering from psychotic illness by means of psychoanalysis. He believed that psychotic process led to a withdrawal of all libidinal cathexes from the object and the external world, resulting in lack of transference relationship to the analyst. Today we know that this is not the case and even Freud's position evolved over time, and in his interpretation of Schreber's memoirs (1911) the idea of transference is already present. Moreover, in the posthumously published An Outline of Psychoanalysis, Freud says:

The problem of psychoses would be simple and intelligible if the withdrawal of the ego from reality could be carried through completely. But that seems rarely if ever to happen. Even in conditions so far removed from the reality of the external world as hallucinatory confusional states, one learns from patients after their recovery that at the time in some corner of their minds, as they express it, there was a normal person hidden, who watched the hubbub of the illness go past, like a disinterested spectator. (Freud, 1946, pp. 114-15)

Here I think lie the origins of the questions raised today by Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz, that is, what is the place of psychoanalysis in the understanding and treatment of psychoses, what is the appropriate setting and analytic technique, what is the relationship between psychosis and neurosis, and the fate of symbol formation? What are the dominant defence mechanisms and the significance of unconscious phantasy?

Following the contributions of Karl Abraham (1911) and Melanie Klein (1946), Hanna Segal (1950) described her work with a schizophrenic patient treated in a largely traditional psychoanalytic setting, that is, five sessions per week and on the couch, making a strong case for psychoanalysis as a treatment for psychosis, provided there is sufficient external support. Around the same time, in the United States, Gustav Bychowski (1952) published his Psychotherapy of Psychosis and in 1955 Jacques Lacan gave his seminar on psychotic processes, emphasizing deficits in emotional development, psychic structure and symbolization due to the foreclosure of the Name-of-the-Father (Lacan, 1993). Wilfred Bion (1962), on the other hand, introduced his concept of alpha function, pointing to the importance of the capacity to metabolize raw sensuous and emotional data from the outside and the inside of the body, in order to form the mind with its contact barrier and enable processes such as repression, dreaming and symbolization.

Psychosis and the Limits of Language

Christos Tombras PHD

Christos Tombras

christos.tombras@listeningtoyou.co.uk

Christos Tombras   Lacanian psychoanalyst and clinical supervisor, practising in London. He is a member of the Centre for Freudian Analysis and Research (CFAR) and also of the College of Psychoanalysts - UK. As a regular speaker at CFAR's public lectures programme and elsewhere, and in his writings, he explores the possibility of a dialogue between contemporary continental philosophy and psychoanalysis. In his clinical work, he is especially interested in questions of psychosis - the term understood in its Lacanian conceptualization. He has worked extensively with people suffering from psychosis, both in his private practice, but also in the NHS and in the private sector. He is currently contributing to the work of the Psychosis Therapy Project as a clinical supervisor.

The title of today's conference, Psychosis and Psychoanalysis, draws our attention to this most serious of questions for a psychoanalyst, namely the question of whether his or her tools are appropriate to treat psychosis. Or, to put it in another way, whether psychosis is indeed within the reach of psychoanalytic technique. This was the central theme of Dorothée's clinical presentation, and I am in agreement with her position when she tells us that ‘If anything, psychosis is at the very core of the psychoanalytic project’.

As I understand it, this question depends on another one, which, to evoke the title of one of Lacan's core texts on psychosis (Lacan, 2006b), is a question ‘prior to any possible treatment of psychosis’. To put it simply, Lacan invites us to think just that: What is Psychosis? How do we understand psychosis?

In her clinical presentation, Dorothée brought the example of those psychotic subjects who, experiencing as it seems a sense of bodily fragmentation, attempt to keep things together by wrapping themselves ‘in multiple layers of clothes’, attempting to survive, as it were, ‘an unamendable state of being “in bits and pieces”’. These patients seem to feel very unsafe in their bodily experience. They appear as if trying to keep themselves together, using their clothes.

I was reminded, in this connection, of Judge Daniel Paul Schreber, and especially of chapter 11 of his Memoirs, entitled ‘Bodily integrity damaged by miracles’ (Schreber, 2000, pp. 141-51) - a chapter dedicated to questions of anxiety because of bodily fragmentation and to his hallucinatory interpretations of these experiences.1

The Witch as a Psychological Figure

Nick Humphreys

Nick Humphreys

[nickhumps@hotmail.co.uk]

Nick Humphreys   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist. He is a qualified member of South Trent, a Midlands-based NHS psychotherapy training organization. He has worked in NHS mental health services in Leicester for over 30 years, specifically in a therapeutic community for personality disorders and as an adult psychotherapist in the Leicester Dynamic Psychotherapy Service. He has worked as a supervisor and trainer and has led the analytical psychology seminars of the South Trent training programme. He has contributed to publications on therapeutic communities, staff support groups and research into the efficacy of Balint groups. He is currently working in private practice in Leicester.
WITCH, EXCLUSION, SUBJUGATION, DEFENCE, CREATIVITY, TRANSMUTATION

Using a Jungian perspective, this paper considers the psychological figure of the witch in analytic work with two male patients. The witch emerged as a personification of the patient's complexes in the transference and countertransference, and in the content of dreams, images, and other objects of association. The witch presided over experiences of captivity and captivation, an object of fear for one man and a seductive figure for the other. The witch was also a potential transformative agent and path of psychological development, revealing the creativity of the archetype in the core of the complex. This dual function is highlighted with reference to the Grimm story of Hansel and Gretel and Jung's concept of the transcendent function. The clinical material gives some consideration as to whether or not the witch can be engaged for a therapeutic development involving the integration of the complex. Both men were seen for up to two years in an NHS psychotherapy service.

From the Couch to the Circle: Group-Analytic Psychotherapy in Practice by John R. Schlaporbersky. Published by Routledge, London, 2016; 528 pp, £37.99 paperback.

Stephen Arcari

Stephen Arcari

[stephen_arcari@hotmail.com]

Stephen Arcari  

In this excellent book John Schlaporbersky shares his wisdom gleaned from many years of group analytic practice. From the Couch to the Circle explores the changes in theory and technique needed to move from therapy with individual patients (couch) to working with a group of patients (circle) while staying within a psychoanalytic model. Schlaporbersky also successfully tackles the challenge of drawing together Foulkes' original discoveries into a practical textbook of group analysis as a method for the treatment of mental distress and the transformation of personal unhappiness. The book communicates his wide-ranging understanding of psychoanalytic psychotherapy.

The book is clearly divided into three sections: 1. Foundations; 2. The Group Analytic Model; 3. Dynamics of Change.

In Section 1 (which is around half of the book), Schlaporbersky introduces the reader to psychotherapy in general. This is no small task as not only does he have to draw comparisons between theories of the individual and theories of the group, but he also has to take account of the changing focus in both fields. Finding correspondence between individual theories with their early roots in drive theory and an intra-psychic focus, and group theories that rely on interaction between individuals and relational patterns that develop is challenging. However, the author is clearly someone who grasps similarities between ideas. The development of a relational model of psychoanalysis over the last 30 years has also helped bridge the theories of individual and group methods of psychotherapy (Tubert-Oklander, 2014).

No one who knows the author's clinical work would be surprised to find that there is a strong emphasis on the role and characteristics of communication in the psychotherapeutic process.

In Chapter 4, ‘The Language of the Group’ he reminds us of his important linking of forms of speech: monologue, dialogue and discourse with psychological forms, that is, one-person psychology, two-person psychology and three-person psychology. This work is developed in Chapter 5 where Schlaporbersky looks at speech and silence in psychotherapy, developing and deepening the themes of the previous chapters. By exploring the relationship between these two seemingly opposite forms of communication he shows how a well established group's functioning can move between the everyday world and a transformational space.
